videos.script: Every test so far compared groups. This lesson asks a different question: when one number goes up, does another go up with it? {{question}} Take Horta's hundred and twenty deliveries. Put distance along the bottom and minutes up the side, and draw one dot per delivery. The dots form a band that climbs from left to right. Longer trips take longer. {{band}} A correlation coefficient puts that picture into one number, between minus one and one. Plus one is a perfect rising line. Minus one is a perfect falling line. Zero is no straight-line pattern at all. For distance and minutes, it is point nine one. {{number}} That number is useful, and it is easy to misread. Four famous data sets share the same correlation and look nothing alike. A single delivery far from the rest can create a correlation out of nothing, or hide one that is there. {{misread}} So this lesson comes in a fixed order. Draw the points first. Compute the number second. And if the pattern curves, or a few points sit far from the rest, use a version built on ranks, which a single wild value cannot drag around. {{order}}
